summary: Nepal grants a visa on arrival to almost every nationality — 30 USD for 15 days, 50 USD for 30 days or 125 USD for 90 days, all multiple entry and extendable — while Indian citizens cross the open border freely without a visa. An optional online form speeds up the arrival queue.

declarations.name: Online Tourist Visa Application (pre-arrival form)
declarations.text: Optional but recommended: fill in the tourist visa 'Online Application' at nepaliport.immigration.gov.np before you fly and bring the printed receipt/barcode. It replaces the airport kiosk step and shortens the visa-on-arrival queue.

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency over 5,000 USD in cash (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival. Import and export of Nepali rupees by foreign nationals is restricted, and Indian rupee notes of 500 and 2,000 INR are not permitted in Nepal.

notes: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 1.15 litres of spirits per adult.
Drones may not be brought in and flown without prior permits; satellite phones also require authorisation.

payments.text: Cash rules everywhere outside upmarket Kathmandu and Pokhara hotels and restaurants. On trekking routes there are no card facilities and few ATMs — carry enough rupees for the whole trek.

safety.text: Nepal is generally safe and welcoming, with petty theft the main urban risk. The real hazards are environmental: altitude sickness, mountain weather, road conditions and occasional strikes (bandhs) that halt transport.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Nepal Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: October–November (post-monsoon, clearest skies) and March–April (rhododendron spring) are the classic trekking seasons. Winter is cold at altitude; June to September is monsoon.

tips.text: Most treks need permits on top of your visa: a TIMS card and/or national park or conservation area fees (Annapurna, Sagarmatha, Langtang), and restricted areas like Upper Mustang require special permits arranged through a registered agency.
Buy insurance that explicitly covers trekking at your maximum altitude and helicopter evacuation. Standard policies often stop at 3,000 m — well below Everest Base Camp or the Thorong La.
Bring the visa fee in cash (USD preferred, crisp notes). Card payment and the airport kiosks are unreliable — pre-filling the online form at nepaliport.immigration.gov.np saves a long queue.
Overstaying costs 3 USD per day plus fines and can mean being barred from future entry — extend at the Department of Immigration in Kathmandu or Pokhara before your visa runs out.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Nepal?
faq.answer: Yes, but it is issued on arrival: US passport holders (like almost all nationalities) get a tourist visa at Kathmandu airport or any land border — 30 USD for 15 days, 50 USD for 30 days or 125 USD for 90 days, multiple entry. Bring the fee in cash.

faq.question: Do Indian citizens need a visa for Nepal?
faq.answer: No. Under the 1950 India–Nepal friendship treaty the border is open: Indian citizens enter without a visa and without stay limits, using a passport or accepted identity document (airlines require a passport, voter ID or other approved ID for flights).

faq.question: How does Nepal's visa on arrival work?
faq.answer: On arrival you complete a form (or bring the receipt from the free online form at nepaliport.immigration.gov.np, submitted within 15 days before travel), pay the fee in cash and receive the visa sticker. Queues at Kathmandu airport can be long — the pre-filled form and exact cash speed things up.

faq.question: Can I extend my Nepal tourist visa?
faq.answer: Yes, at the Department of Immigration in Kathmandu or Pokhara: minimum 45 USD for 15 days, then 3 USD per day, up to a maximum of 150 days in Nepal per calendar year.

faq.question: Do I need permits for trekking in Nepal besides the visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Most routes require a TIMS card and/or national park or conservation area entry fees (for example Sagarmatha for Everest, ACAP for Annapurna), and restricted regions such as Upper Mustang or Manaslu need special permits obtained through a registered trekking agency, sometimes with a mandatory guide.
